common_name: Happy Trails Fuchsia Portulaca (Vigorous Trailing Moss Rose)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery starts after the last frost into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; this vegetatively propagated color of the trailing Happy Trails line is not grown from seed.

directions: Transplant rooted cuttings after the last frost into lean, sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun, since rich or soggy ground encourages stem rot instead of bloom. Happy Trails Fuchsia produces vivid magenta-pink double flowers over trailing succulent stems, making it a strong spiller for hanging baskets, window boxes, and the edges of raised beds. Water only when the soil has dried out completely, then soak thoroughly, since this cultivar is bred to shrug off extended dry spells once its roots are established. Pinch back leggy stems in midsummer to encourage denser branching and a fresh flush of color for fall.

common_name: Happy Trails Yellow Portulaca (Vigorous Trailing Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after the last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; like other Happy Trails colors this is not offered as seed.

directions: Set transplants after the last frost into lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun. Happy Trails Yellow bears frilly, gold-eyed double flowers along cascading stems clothed in tiny succulent leaves, spilling gracefully from hanging baskets or over the edges of a container. It flowers most fully in direct sun and closes on heavily overcast days, so avoid shaded plantings if continuous color is the goal. Because it stores water in its fleshy tissue, established plantings tolerate being missed on the watering schedule far better than most bedding annuals.

common_name: Happy Trails Deep Red Portulaca (Vigorous Trailing Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated starts after the last frost in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this color is sold as rooted cuttings or finished plants rather than seed.

directions: Transplant into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost has passed. Happy Trails Deep Red carries intensely saturated, semi-double crimson blooms over a fast-spreading trailing habit, giving hanging baskets and window boxes a bold splash of color through the hottest part of summer. Allow the growing medium to dry between waterings, since consistently damp soil is far more likely to kill this cultivar than drought. Its short-day flowering trait lets it bud up and bloom earlier in spring than older seed-grown moss rose types.
sources: GrowerFacts Portulaca Happy Trails F1 Series

common_name: Mojave Fuchsia Portulaca (Large-Flowered Drought-Tolerant Moss Rose)

planting.note: Set out transplants after the last frost into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; Mojave was bred for unusually large blooms on a mounding, non-trailing habit.

directions: Plant in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, since damp or fertile ground quickly leads to rot and weak flowering. Mojave Fuchsia produces oversized magenta-pink blooms that hold their color well in intense summer heat, sitting atop a tight, mounding plant rather than sprawling loosely like older moss rose strains. It shrugs off extended dry stretches once established and rarely needs supplemental irrigation outside of prolonged drought. Deadheading is unnecessary, as spent flowers are quickly hidden by the next flush of buds opening in bright sun.

planting.note: Surface-sow after the last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; do not cover the seed, since it needs light to germinate. Sundial Fuchsia stays open later in the day and on overcast afternoons than older moss rose strains.

directions: Scatter seed on the surface of lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, pressing it in lightly without covering. Sundial Fuchsia produces vivid magenta-pink double blooms on a compact, early-flowering mound, part of a breeding line selected to remain open through overcast weather when older portulaca varieties would stay closed. Once established it needs almost no supplemental water and actually performs best when kept on the dry side between rains. Thin seedlings to about 8 inches apart to let the mounds fill in without crowding.

common_name: Sundial Peppermint Portulaca (Bicolor Striped Moss Rose)

planting.note: Surface-sow after the last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; do not cover the fine seed, which needs light to germinate.

directions: Sow seed directly on lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, since it germinates only when exposed to light. Sundial Peppermint bears white petals splashed and streaked with hot pink in an irregular candy-cane pattern, with each flower marked slightly differently from the next, and it holds its blooms open later in the day than older moss rose strains. The compact, spreading mound tolerates prolonged neglect and poor soil far better than regular watering and rich beds, so err on the side of underwatering. Remove any surrounding mulch that shades the crown, since Sundial types flower most heavily where the soil surface stays warm and dry.

planting.note: Surface-sow after the last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; press seed into the surface without covering it, since portulaca needs light to germinate.

directions: Direct sow on the surface of lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun once the last frost has passed. Sundial Tangerine covers its compact mound in bright orange double flowers that stay open well into the afternoon and on overcast days, unlike many older moss rose seed strains that close by early afternoon. It thrives in poor, gravelly soil and actually declines in rich or consistently damp beds, so hold back on fertilizer and irrigation once seedlings are established. A light shearing partway through summer can refresh the mound and extend flowering into fall.

common_name: Cupcake Yellow Chrome Portulaca (Vegetative Mounding Moss Rose)

planting.note: Plant vegetatively propagated liners or finished plants after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Cupcake is a fast-finishing series bred for strong branching without pinching.

directions: Transplant into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing plants to let their naturally bushy habit fill in without staking. Cupcake Yellow Chrome forms a dense, floriferous mound of bright chrome-yellow blooms over succulent foliage and, true to its breeding, seems to flower more heavily as summer heat intensifies rather than slowing down. It requires little pinching or grooming compared with older portulaca types and needs only occasional deep watering once its roots are established in the bed or container. Avoid overhead irrigation late in the day, since wet foliage overnight can invite fungal problems in humid Gulf Coast summers.
sources: Greenhouse Product News — Crop Culture Report: Portulaca Cupcake Series

common_name: Cupcake Carrot Portulaca (Vegetative Mounding Moss Rose)

planting.note: Set out rooted liners or finished plants after the last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this cultivar is propagated vegetatively rather than grown from seed.

directions: Plant in lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, since this series was trialed successfully in record summer heat across the Gulf South and Southeast. Cupcake Carrot produces warm orange blooms over a compact, well-branched mound that holds its shape in containers and hanging baskets without frequent grooming. It tolerates being allowed to dry out fully between waterings and generally performs poorly if kept in constantly moist soil. From a rooted liner, plants finish quickly, typically filling a 4-inch pot with flowering growth within about five weeks under warm conditions.
sources: Greenhouse Product News — Crop Culture Report: Portulaca Cupcake Series
